record.paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
record.original_question: Can the Tolman surface-brightness test provide a decisive observational distinction between an expanding universe and a non-expanding universe when the observed surface-brightness dependence on redshift must be disentangled from galaxy luminosity evolution, intergalactic absorption by metals or dust, and possible methodological errors?

evidence.quote: Expansion model predicts a (1 + z)−4 dependence, and must therefore invoke special ad hoc evolution to close the gap between theory and observations. This makes the Tolman test useless since we cannot separate its results from the evolution of galaxies.

We do not know how large it is but we must bear in mind that before we know it, we will not be able to contrast the different cosmological hypotheses. Errors due to inaccuracies of the method are also possible.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider two competing cosmological hypotheses for a population of galaxies observed at varying redshifts z:

(A) An expanding-universe hypothesis, in which the bolometric surface brightness (flux per unit solid angle) of a galaxy of intrinsic luminosity and physical size satisfies the relation SB(z) ∝ (1+z)^(−4) at fixed rest-frame band, in addition to any intrinsic evolution of the source.

(B) A non-expanding (static) universe hypothesis, in which cosmological redshift arises from some non-expansion mechanism and the surface brightness has at most a mild redshift dependence (e.g. SB(z) ∝ (1+z)^0 or (1+z)^(−1) depending on the assumed photon mechanism), modulo intrinsic evolution and absorption.

Let m(z) denote the observed mean surface brightness of a chosen class of galaxies (e.g. early-type galaxies or another standard set) as a function of redshift. Suppose the observed signal decomposes as
   m(z) = T(z) + E(z) + A(z) + η(z),
where T(z) is the cosmological Tolman term (which differs between hypotheses (A) and (B)), E(z) is the contribution from intrinsic luminosity and size evolution of the galaxy population, A(z) is dimming due to intergalactic absorption by dust and metals, and η(z) represents systematic and methodological errors (e.g. point-spread function effects, ellipticity, selection, K-corrections).

Problem. Determine whether, on the basis of currently available or foreseeable photometric data over a wide range of redshifts, the Tolman surface-brightness test can in principle yield a statistically decisive observational discrimination between hypotheses (A) and (B). Specifically:

1. Identify whether E(z), A(z), and η(z) can be independently constrained to a precision sufficient that the residual m(z) − E(z) − A(z) − η(z) distinguishes the predicted (1+z)^(−4) law from the static-universe prediction at high confidence.

2. If not, exhibit a model-independent argument or example showing that any expansion signature can be mimicked by an admissible choice of luminosity evolution E(z) (together with absorption A(z)), so that the test cannot separate cosmological expansion from galaxy evolution.

State precisely the conditions on E(z), A(z), and the observational sample under which the Tolman test is or is not a decisive cosmological discriminator.
artifact.status_search_result: The question remains actively debated. Recent analyses (including JWST-era studies in 2024–2026 using thousands of spectroscopically confirmed galaxies) report that observed surface-brightness trends with redshift depart from the (1+z)^(−4) prediction of the expanding-universe model, but the interpretation is still confounded by uncertain galaxy luminosity/size evolution and intergalactic absorption. No consensus has emerged that the Tolman test decisively distinguishes expanding from non-expanding cosmologies; the degeneracy with evolution remains the central obstacle.

status_evidence.title: Cosmological Observational Tests in the JWST Era. II: The Tolman Test
status_evidence.snippet: Analysis of 6,860 ASTRODEEP-JWST galaxies finds the observed surface-brightness trend departs significantly from the standard cosmological prediction.
status_evidence.claim: As of 2026 the Tolman test's decisive status is still contested and depends on evolution modeling.

status_evidence.title: Observations contradict galaxy size and surface brightness predictions based on the expanding universe hypothesis
status_evidence.snippet: Reports tension between observed surface brightness/size relations and expanding-universe predictions absent strong evolution.
status_evidence.claim: Disentangling evolution from cosmological dimming is unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Tolman surface brightness test - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Describes the test and the ongoing role of galaxy evolution corrections in interpreting results.
status_evidence.claim: Conclusion of the test continues to depend on assumed evolutionary corrections.
